title: 'Parent anxiety' over SEND reforms sees EHCP demand surge even more
excerpt: An increase in applications for Education, Health and Care Plans is adding to pressure as Brent Council faces a £21million SEND funding shortfall
content:
'Parent anxiety' over SEND reforms helps create funding black hole as EHCP demand surges in Brent

An increase in applications for Education, Health and Care Plans is adding to pressure as Brent Council faces a £21million SEND funding shortfall

11:21, 15 Nov 2026

A surge in applications for EHCPs has led to a potential multimillion-pound funding gap for SEND in Brent, partly driven by parents' concerns over national reforms.

‌

‌

There has been a 10% rise in the number of children requiring Education, Health and Care Plans in the past year, bringing the total in the borough to 4,437. Brent Council faces a funding shortfall for special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) of £20.8million by March 31, 2027, as reported by the Brent Council Schools Forum on Tuesday, November 10.

‌

The mounting deficit comes after financial interventions by the council helped cover the historic shortfalls following the approval of its Local SEND Reform Plan. The authority secured an £18.2m high-needs stability grant from the Department for Education, with the remaining £2m covered by a local revenue support grant and other surpluses.

‌

Yet while the demand for EHCPs has grown, funding has not increased, creating financial pressures for local authorities.

Carol Foyle, the Parent Participation Coordinator for Brent Parent Carer Forum, reported that they have seen a rise in parent-led applications for EHCPs due to their anxieties ahead of incoming national SEND reforms. She said: "We are seeing an increase in parental requests and a slight decrease in school requests [where the school recommends a child gets an EHCP], but I think the parental requests are because of quite a lot of anxiety about the reforms that are coming in.

‌

"There is very much in Brent an awareness of the situation and what we can do when the money isn't there, but they are not a borough that is one to cut. They have just launched the Experts at Hand, which should help this. What we're picking up is that parents are in a really low state of mood because of the reforms, really."

Brent's 'Experts at Hand' model will help build specialist capacity in mainstream classrooms.

‌

The Government's SEND reforms are aimed at ensuring many children with additional needs are able to stay in mainstream school settings, with appropriate support. But there is concern some kids who need more specialist interventions could be deprived of a specialist school place, and that funding for support in mainstream schools could be stretched. As EHCPs are legally binding, theoretically schools should prioritise any pupils who have one, for additional support.

Government support for this new deficit in Brent has not yet been guaranteed, with the Department for Education warning that future bailouts "will not be unlimited" and will depend on Brent's delivery of SEND reform targets.

‌

There has been a sharp increase in demand for EHCPs in the borough, with growth of 10% from September 2025 to 2026, up from 8% the year before.

The forecast funding gap of £20.8m over the next year has been driven up by a range of pressures, including out-of-borough school placements, post-16 placements, a shortage of local specialist places, increased demand for children receiving education otherwise than at school, such as home schooling, or awaiting a specialist placement.

‌

Nigel Chapman, Corporate Director for Children, Young People and Community Development, stated in the report: "The council continues to focus on sufficiency of places, reducing reliance on external placements and ensuring services remain financially sustainable.

"Oversight is provided directly with the Corporate Director of Finance to coordinate demand management, expand local provision, and roll out the 'Experts at Hand' support model."

Brent is delivering an approved Local SEND Reform Plan focused on expanding the number of in-borough special school places and settings with additional SEND resources, to reduce their reliance on costly out-of-borough placements.
